title: Size-Glide: Reversible Tailoring for GLP-1 Wardrobes
one_liner: Prepaid mail-in take-in tailoring, done with reversible seams, that follows a GLP-1 patient down (and back up) through 3-5 sizes, sold as a retention perk to the telehealth programs that prescribe the drugs.
customer: Two payers. (1) Consumers in months 3-18 of GLP-1 treatment, mostly women 35-60 with a professional wardrobe worth $2-5k. (2) GLP-1 telehealth and employer weight-management programs, who pay a per-member fee because churn is their biggest cost.
problem: Patients drop 2-5 sizes in a year. Buying a new wardrobe at each stage costs $1-3k. Local tailors are slow, inconsistent and expensive, and permanent take-ins ruin a garment when weight comes back. Roughly half of users stop within a year and most regain, so the wardrobe problem repeats in both directions. Programs also lack a tangible, celebratory milestone reward that keeps people enrolled.
solution: A prepaid alteration bag ships to your door. A vetted network of micro-tailors runs a standardized 12-garment menu (waist, hem, darts, sleeves) using reversible methods: basted or removable seams and preserved allowances. Every garment gets a QR tag and a digital 'garment passport' recording each alteration and its size band. Weight milestones trigger reminders ('you are down 15 lb, send the blazers'). A let-out service and a resale or donate-out handoff handle regain and garments that are now too big. Telehealth partners can offer 'your first three take-ins are free' as a milestone reward.
why_now: The Wegovy pill launched in January 2026 and Lilly's oral drug is rolling out this year. GLP-1 households now command roughly $660B in spending power (Numerator, August 2026). Employer coverage and cost pressure are creating start-stop cycles, which makes reversible work the safer product.
revenue_model: Prepaid alteration packs of $250-600 per stage, or a $39-79/month wardrobe plan. B2B2C: $10-25 per member per month from telehealth and employer programs as a retention benefit. Small margin on resale handoffs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not clothing, it is tailor turnaround and the trust that a garment can come back to its old size. Reversibility is the moat because regain is the norm, not the exception. The best paying customer is the telehealth company's churn budget, not the patient.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 alteration shops in one metro and write a 12-item price menu. Post in r/Zepbound and r/Ozempic communities and local GLP-1 clinic groups to sell 50 prepaid packs. Run a pilot with one small GLP-1 clinic or telehealth startup using free milestone take-ins. Use QR tags and a spreadsheet for the garment passport, and courier pickup for logistics.

title: Paid Neighbor Walking Routes for Absent Kids
one_liner: Hire retired neighbors and parents as paid 'route captains' who walk or wake up chronically absent kids on fixed blocks, and get paid a share of the funding that the recovered attendance brings back.
customer: Principals and districts in states that fund schools on average daily attendance (California, Texas and similar). Secondary payers are city safe-passage budgets, Title I funds and Medicaid plans (for asthma and chronic-condition kids).
problem: About one in four kids is chronically absent. Nudge letters and text campaigns work on the 10 to 19 day group but barely touch the kids missing 25 or more days. For them it is a 7:40 a.m. logistics problem: a parent working an early shift, an older sibling who moved on to middle school, a dangerous corner, no clean clothes, no alarm clock. In attendance-funded states, each absent day costs the school roughly what a day of instruction is worth, so a $200-per-kid fix pays back several times over.
solution: Micro-employ 3 to 5 route captains per school as part-time W-2 workers (7:00 to 8:30 a.m., roughly $18 an hour). Each captain covers a block-by-block route, walking 6 to 10 kids, knocking on doors, and running a breakfast and laundry pass. Captains report barrier codes by voice note, which feed the attendance team's dashboard. Contract as a base route fee plus 20 to 25 percent of documented funding gains from improved attendance.
why_now: Chronic absenteeism has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. ESSER-funded attendance staff were cut as that money expired. States now require chronic-absence plans, and the retiree and gig-worker labor pool is looking for short, local, part-time work.
revenue_model: Base fee per route plus a performance share of recovered attendance funding. Optional per-route sponsorship from health plans or employers.
non_obvious_insight: Districts spend on software and letters, but the students who cost the most are the ones for whom the 7:40 a.m. logistics fail. The cheapest fix is a grandmother on the corner, and it is invisible to edtech buyers because it is not a product. The first three Mondays of September predict the year, so contracting has to start before October.
first_30_days: Pilot with one principal in an attendance-funded state: 2 routes, about 12 kids, 4 part-time captains recruited from churches and senior centers. Establish baselines from last year's attendance data and track days present weekly. Write the performance addendum as a one-page contract that a principal can sign with discretionary funds and later convert to a district contract.

title: ITAR-Safe Identity for New-Space Startups
one_liner: An identity layer that proves a new hire is real, where they actually are and whether they may legally see spacecraft technical data, then feeds that attribute straight into SSO and PLM access controls.
customer: Series A-C launch, satellite and defense-space startups (50-500 staff) and their sub-tier machine shops and avionics suppliers, reached through space-focused investors, accelerators and SpaceWERX/SBIR cohorts. Buyers are the head of security or compliance and the CFO.
problem: Space startups are hiring at breakneck speed, with remote engineers and contractors, into a Golden Dome-driven market (cost estimate raised to $185B) and nine-figure funding rounds. Giving a foreign person access to technical data is an ITAR export violation, and North Korean IT-worker schemes have reached 70 to 100+ US companies. Standard IDV proves someone is real, not whether they are a US person, and HR and ATS tools do not carry export-control eligibility as an access attribute. Fake suppliers and counterfeit parts add a second exposure.
solution: (1) Verify person and US-person status using document and injection-resistant liveness (partner with an existing IDV vendor rather than building it). (2) Check presence over time (VPN and laptop-farm signals). (3) Write 'US person, permitted data categories' into Okta or Entra groups and PLM and repo permissions through SCIM. (4) Supplier onboarding with KYB, sanctions and counterfeit-part red flags. (5) An auditor-ready evidence pack for CMMC Level 2 assessments and export-compliance reviews.
why_now: The DoD's CMMC rollout reaches its second phase on 10 Nov 2026, when third-party Level 2 certification starts appearing in contracts, and small suppliers are scrambling. North Korean worker prosecutions in Apr and May 2026 put hiring fraud on boards' agendas, while 3-second voice cloning and virtual-camera injection attacks defeat casual video interviews.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified person per year, $1-3K per month platform fee, and $250 per supplier onboarding. Add a paid $2K 'ITAR access audit' as an entry product.
non_obvious_insight: In space the compliance object is not employee identity but nationality-scoped access to technical data. The unbuilt gap is attribute-based access control fed by identity proof into CAD and PLM systems. These startups fear DDTC and DoD audits and investor diligence more than hackers, so they buy compliance evidence rather than security.
first_30_days: Build a 'verified US person to Okta group' integration on an off-the-shelf IDV API. Sell a $2K ITAR access audit (export the Drive, GitHub and PLM permission lists and flag foreign-person exposures) to 5 startups via investor and accelerator introductions in Colorado Springs, Los Angeles and Huntsville. Convert audits to per-seat subscriptions before the Nov 2026 CMMC milestone.

title: Vacant-Unit Meter Watchdog and Insurance Vacancy Log
one_liner: Uses utility smart-meter data that owners already have rights to, so PMs can catch squatters, leaks and freeze risk in empty units within hours, without installing any hardware.
customer: Property managers and owners of single-family and 2-to-20-unit portfolios (100 to 2,000 doors). They already pay the utilities on vacant units and carry standard dwelling or small-building policies with a vacancy clause. Buyer is the PM's ops director or the owner. Secondary buyers later are E&S and landlord-program insurers.
problem: When a unit is occupied, the tenant is the sensor and tells you about leaks. When it is vacant you are blind for 20 to 60 days. Water damage, squatters, stolen copper, AC left running and burst pipes all happen in that window. Most property policies restrict vandalism, water damage and theft after roughly 60 days of vacancy, and the claim gets denied or cut exactly when the loss is biggest. Squatter removal is also time-critical: in many states an intruder found on day 2 is a police trespass matter, while the same person on day 30 needs a months-long court eviction. Walk-throughs are weekly at best, and the maintenance tech skips them when busy.
solution: Vacancy Vitals connects to interval electric and water data through owner-authorized utility APIs (Green Button Connect, or aggregators like UtilityAPI). The owner's account is usually the one active during vacancy, so no tenant consent is needed. Rules fire on patterns: continuous 24/7 water flow (leak), electric baseline above the empty-unit norm (someone living there, a crypto miner, a grow), a heating or cooling setpoint far outside range (pipe-freeze or mold risk), and a sudden drop to zero in a unit that should be running HVAC. Alerts go by text to the on-call tech with a one-tap 'send someone' button. The product also generates a time-stamped weekly vacancy-inspection log (data check plus a tech photo check-in) formatted for carriers' vacancy-permit or inspection conditions. That log is what preserves coverage.
why_now: Anti-squatter laws were passed in a wave in 2024 and 2025 (for example Florida and Georgia), which makes early detection more valuable. Smart-meter penetration passed roughly 70% of US electric customers. Insurers have been tightening on water-damage and vacancy exposure for several years. AI-based anomaly detection on interval data is now cheap. (Current state-by-state anti-squatter rules and utility API coverage should be verified before launch.)
revenue_model: $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month on usage, or a flat $1 to $2 per door per month portfolio subscription. Later, insurer-paid or insurer-discounted programs: the carrier pays a fee per monitored door in exchange for lower loss ratios and a vacancy-clause waiver.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest sensor for a vacant house is the meter the utility already installed, and the account is in the owner's name during vacancy. Nobody in proptech treats owner-account utility data as a security and insurance-compliance feed. They sell $60 leak sensors and cameras instead. The other secret is legal timing. The value is not detecting the squatter, it is detecting them in the first 48 hours, when the law treats it as trespass rather than a tenancy.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 to 5 SFR or small-multifamily PMs, offer a free 'backtest', and pull 12 months of interval data for units that were vacant. Show them the incidents the tool would have caught. These are usually a few leaks, a few unauthorized occupants and several HVAC-left-on units, each worth $1,000 to $15,000. Build a UtilityAPI-based prototype with three rules, text alerts and a weekly PDF log. Charge $99 per month per portfolio during the pilot, then convert to per-unit pricing. In parallel, talk to two independent insurance agents who write landlord programs, to learn the exact vacancy-permit language and to get a warm intro for the carrier channel.

title: Volumetric Concert Replays for Small Venues
one_liner: A multi-camera Gaussian-splat capture rig that lets attendees of 200-2,000 capacity shows buy a free-viewpoint replay of their favorite songs.
customer: Independent venues, promoters and mid-tier touring acts, with ticket-holders as end buyers at $5-15 per replay.
problem: Small acts earn only from tickets and merch, and concert film needs a crew. Sphere grossed $420.5M in 2024 but is for superstars. Fans want to relive the night from where they stood, and no affordable product delivers it.
solution: A 12-24 camera synced rig hung on lighting truss, cloud splat processing, and a phone and headset web viewer. Attendees unlock replays via a ticket QR code. Start with one or two songs with static cameras and add motion later, with revenue shared with the venue and artist.
why_now: 4D Gaussian splatting hit practical quality and cost in 2025-26, web viewers are mature, and headsets are common enough to matter.
revenue_model: $2-5k capture fee per show or free capture with 50% of replay sales, plus venue subscription for archives.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the film but the fan's own position. Selling 'the replay from where I stood' to the 300 people who attended targets a captive small market with high willingness to pay.
first_30_days: Build a 12-camera rig for about $8k. Capture 3 local shows in exchange for rights. Test QR-code replay sales at the merch table and measure conversion.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Downstream Buyers
one_liner: A contingency recovery-audit firm that claws back tariff surcharges buyers paid on duties their suppliers have since had refunded.
customer: CFOs, AP and purchasing teams at $20M-$1B manufacturers and distributors that paid itemized supplier 'tariff surcharges' in 2025-26.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20. By 2026-07-10 CBP had accepted about $121.75B in claims and repaid about $86.3B. Many suppliers billed explicit surcharges (one shop-floor post cites 2.7%) to fund those duties, and they are now collecting refunds on the same money. Buyers assume the refund belongs to the importer of record, and AP treats surcharge lines as noise.
solution: Ingest 18 months of AP data from the ERP or QuickBooks. Use LLM extraction on invoices and price-increase emails to find surcharge lines. Rank suppliers by likely refunded exposure (product HTS and the IEEPA rate window). Generate credit-memo demands and negotiation scripts. Escalate to counsel only for large amounts. Recovery depends on invoice and contract language, and most cases settle as credits against future invoices.
why_now: Refunds are paying out in phases right now, so suppliers hold the cash today. Contract dispute windows are open and evidence is fresh.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency fee on recovered cash or credits. Optional $5k flat fee for a scan of the last 12 months of AP.
non_obvious_insight: The strongest and cheapest claim to a refund often belongs to the downstream buyer holding an itemized surcharge, not the importer. Recovery-audit firms hunt duplicate payments, not tariffs. Buyers also avoid asking for fear of damaging the supplier relationship, so an anonymous third party has an edge.
first_30_days: Sign 5 mid-market manufacturers for a free 12-month surcharge scan. Have counsel draft one template letter. Send the first demands and measure realized recovery. First credit memos should land within 60-90 days.

title: Ulysses Contracts for AI Use in Psychosis Recovery
one_liner: A patient-signed pre-commitment plus an app that adds friction and alerts a trusted contact when a recovering patient's chatbot use starts to spiral.
customer: Early-psychosis and community mental-health programs ($15-30 per patient per month) and families of people with a prior psychotic or manic episode ($12 a month).
problem: Trend chain: chatbot sycophancy leads to documented chatbot-linked psychosis (UCSF's Keith Sakata treated 12 cases; the Human Line Project spans 22 countries), then people with prior episodes are the most exposed, then clinicians can only say 'avoid chatbots' and families cannot police 3 a.m. sessions. Psychiatric advance directives cover hospitalization, not AI use.
solution: (1) A one-page 'AI Use Advance Directive' completed with the treating clinician while the patient is well. (2) A device-level app that watches patterns locally (late-night sessions, session length and, with consent, on-device classification of grandiose or mission-style themes) and applies escalating friction: delay, grounding script, message to a trusted contact, weekly clinician summary. (3) Data stays on the device except the escalation flag.
why_now: OpenAI's own Oct 2025 estimate (0.07% of weekly users show signs of psychosis or mania) implies hundreds of thousands of people. Regulation is bans and disclosures, not protection at the device level. On-device small models now make private classification feasible, and no lab has to cooperate.
revenue_model: Per-patient monthly licenses to programs (early-psychosis programs have dedicated public funding) and a $12 monthly family plan. Later: payer and long-acting-injectable partner programs.
non_obvious_insight: The winning product is not a smarter chatbot but a pre-commitment device, the same logic as psychiatric advance directives: the well self binds the unwell self. Because it lives at the device layer, it works across every model.
first_30_days: Recruit two early-psychosis programs via clinician advisors. Draft the directive template with them. Build an Android-first usage monitor (fastest to ship) and test it with about 15 patients. Sell programs a $5k pilot.

title: Thermal Commons on Failed Golf Courses
one_liner: Turn shuttered golf courses into shared geothermal borefields that heat and cool the neighborhoods that already surround them.
customer: Gas and electric utilities running thermal-energy-network pilots, housing authorities and multifamily or 55+ community owners next to a course, and the course owner as a land-lease seller.
problem: Networked geothermal works, but it is starved for land. Dense neighborhoods have no room for borefields, so pilots dig up streets or use scraps of parking lots. Meanwhile ~90 golf courses close a year, leaving 100-150 acre owners stuck in expensive rezoning fights with neighbors who hate new housing.
solution: A small developer that (1) screens closed and for-sale courses by distance to heat loads (apartments, schools, 55+ communities) and utility franchise, (2) options the best sites, (3) runs thermal response tests, (4) designs a borefield and neighborhood loop, and (5) sells capacity to the utility or thermal service to buildings under long contracts. The surface stays green as a public park or trails, which turns a NIMBY fight into an amenity and speeds approvals.
why_now: Utility pilots are real and funded. Eversource's Framingham phase 2 has a $7.8M DOE grant with construction in 2026 and launch in early 2027. NYSEG's UTEN pilot in Ithaca and National Grid's Massachusetts approvals add to that. State thermal-network mandates are spreading, and the utility model is still being written, so a site-finder-and-developer has room to define it.
revenue_model: Phase 1 (first six months): paid feasibility and site-screening reports for utilities, cities and housing authorities ($25-80k each, often grant-funded) plus land option fees. Phase 2: own or co-own the borefield asset with availability payments from a utility, or per-building thermal service contracts over 20 years.
non_obvious_insight: Land, not technology, is the bottleneck, and a failed golf course arrives pre-cleared, flat, surrounded by customers and owned by someone losing money. A borefield leaves the surface untouched, so the same acreage can also be the park that gets you the permit. The pitch to a utility is 'we bring you a community-approved site, not a science project'.
first_30_days: Build a GIS screen of ~500 closed or listed courses against multifamily density and utility service areas in states with thermal-network programs (NY, MA, CO, MD, MN, WA). Send data packs on the top 10 sites to utility pilot teams and housing authorities. Land one paid feasibility study and sign two cheap options ($5-20k each).

title: Pre-Engineered Single-Stair Plan Sets
one_liner: License stamped, fire-marshal-ready plan sets for 4-6 story single-stair buildings so small developers can use the new law without a $250K custom design.
customer: Small infill developers, church and nonprofit landowners and small architecture firms in single-stair states, plus modular fabricators.
problem: Seven states reformed single-stair rules in 2025 and Michigan followed in July 2026, promising about 10% cost savings, but architects and fire officials lack templates. Custom design is slow, local amendments add friction, and construction inputs are up 8.9% while multifamily starts fall.
solution: Engineered plan sets (4/5/6-story, 16-40 units, light-frame and mass-timber variants) with structure and MEP, a fire-safety compensation package, code narrative and a pre-meeting deck for local fire marshals. A network of local architects of record adapts them per site, and a per-state cost estimate is included.
why_now: New laws are taking effect (Michigan July 2026) and California AB 2074 awaits signature, while rising costs make small builders desperate for certainty.
revenue_model: $25-45K per plan license, $10-20K adaptation fee, referral fees from lenders and contractors, and a subscription for code updates.
non_obvious_insight: Legalization does not build housing; templates and fire-marshal comfort do. The first stamped precedent in each state becomes the local pattern, and plan sets have near-zero marginal cost.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed architect who has single-stair experience. Draft one 4-story 16-unit set for Michigan. Presell three licenses to small developers at a $15K founder price and schedule a meeting with one fire marshal.

title: One Annual Fee for Every Mandatory EU Representative
one_liner: A roll-up of small EU authorised-representative shops that bundles every legally required local presence (GDPR Art. 27, AI Act, Data Act, product safety, CRA) into one liability-bearing annual contract for non-EU companies.
customer: US, UK, Israeli, Indian and Asian SaaS, AI and hardware companies ($2M-$200M revenue) selling in the EU without an EU entity. Bought by founders, GCs and ops leads.
problem: Several EU regimes require non-EU companies to name someone in the EU who can be held to account: GDPR Art. 27, AI Act authorised representatives for high-risk and GPAI providers, Data Act legal representative, product-safety responsible person, an optional CRA authorised representative (background knowledge; verify each). Today each comes from a different vendor, many are one-person shops or law firms wary of liability, and none coordinate.
solution: Acquire three to six small rep businesses (typically hundreds to a couple thousand clients on sticky annual fees), keep their brands, and rebuild operations with automation for inbound regulator and data-subject mail triage, translation and escalation. Add an EU law-firm panel as backstop and sell one bundle with a shared register of representations, one invoice and standard playbooks, priced for the liability.
why_now: GPAI duties applied Aug 2025 with enforcement from Aug 2026, Data Act obligations arrived Sep 2025 and Sep 2026, and CRA reporting started 11 Sep 2026, so many non-EU firms suddenly face three or four rep obligations at once. AI lowers the cost of delivering the service.
revenue_model: EUR 3-15k/year per client bundle, 70-80% renewal, acquisitions at roughly 1-2x revenue, and upsell to compliance retainers.
non_obvious_insight: When AI makes drafting free, the scarce good is someone in the EU who can be sued. Liability-bearing presence has pricing power and stickiness, and becoming the address regulators write to is a distribution moat.
first_30_days: List 30 small EU rep providers and approach five owners about a white-label or revenue-share deal that leads to acquisition. Sell the bundle to 10 US SaaS and AI firms through founder communities at EUR 4k and obtain a professional-indemnity quote.

title: Peptide Assurance Mark for Clinics and Processors
one_liner: Independent lot testing and supplier audit with a QR-verifiable mark that lets peptide sellers pass payment-processor and insurer underwriting.
customer: 503A compounding pharmacies, peptide and longevity clinic chains, and the payment processors and insurers who need evidence to underwrite them.
problem: HHS moved ~14 of 19 Category 2 peptides (BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu and others) back toward compoundable in Feb 2026, and an FDA panel backed BPC-157 and KPV on Jul 23. Clinics are multiplying, but Stripe and card networks exclude the category and Forbes (Jun 30, 2026) called it a '$1 billion industry banks won't touch'. Losing a merchant account kills sellers faster than FDA action.
solution: ISO 17025 lab partners test identity, purity, endotoxin, sterility and potency per lot. Supplier and chain-of-custody audits feed a public registry and QR verification that processors, insurers and state boards can accept, with annual certification and monitoring.
why_now: The legal window opened in 2026 with no infrastructure. Purity is uneven, and processors need third-party evidence to underwrite certified merchants.
revenue_model: $250-600 per lot test, $5-15k/year certification, and processor referral fees for certified merchants.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is payments and insurance, not FDA. A credible independent mark is the key that unlocks mainstream merchant accounts, so processors are the hidden buyer.
first_30_days: Contract an accredited lab and run a blind-purchase audit of 30 popular BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products, published as a report. Sell $500 audits to 10 clinics and approach two high-risk processors about fast-tracking certified merchants.

title: Battery-Buffered Induction Kitchens for LPG-Starved Restaurants
one_liner: A load-sharing controller and optional battery lets Indian cloud kitchens and restaurants switch from scarce LPG to induction without waiting months for a utility load upgrade, then pools the fleet as a lunch-and-dinner-peak resource for DISCOMs.
customer: Cloud kitchens, small restaurant chains (5-50 outlets), hostel and office messes, caterers and sweet shops in Indian metros and tier-2 cities.
problem: The Hormuz-driven LPG shortage pushed induction cooktop demand up 20-25x and the government is distributing 500k stoves, but a commercial kitchen converting needs roughly 15-40 kW of extra connected load. DISCOM sanctioned-load upgrades and neighborhood transformers are slow and constrained, and the switch could add up to 27 GW of national demand at the evening peak. Low-income uptake is reported as sluggish because grid and financing are not ready.
solution: A CT-clamp controller (about $300-400) that sequences burners so total draw stays under the sanctioned load, since cooking tolerates duty-cycling. Add a 20-60 kWh LFP buffer to cover lunch and dinner peaks, financed as a monthly cooking-energy subscription through an NBFC and charged off-peak or on midday solar. The aggregated fleet later sells peak flexibility to DISCOMs under state demand-side management programs.
why_now: LPG scarcity is forcing commercial conversion now, stationary LFP packs are around $70/kWh, smart-meter and demand-side management programs are rolling out, and utilities cannot build capacity fast enough (transformer lead times, capex-biased regulation).
revenue_model: Controller sale of INR 25-35k, battery lease or subscription of roughly INR 15-30k per month (benchmarked against the commercial LPG bill it replaces, when LPG is available at all), and later DISCOM peak-flex payments per kW-year plus midday-charging arbitrage.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to electrifying cooking is not the stove but the permission to draw power at the kitchen's meter. A battery and a scheduler turn an infrastructure-approval problem into a financing problem. Cooking is a rare thermal load that can be shaped without harming the product, so the cheap controller does most of the work and generates the data that later sells flexibility.
first_30_days: Sell 10 controllers to cloud kitchens in one metro through restaurant associations and cloud-kitchen operator WhatsApp groups. Log load data and outages, then lease batteries to the first 3 with an NBFC partner. Use the aggregated load data to open a sandbox conversation with one DISCOM.

title: Asset Provenance Ledger for AI Disclosure
one_liner: A plugin for Blender, Photoshop, Unity and Unreal that logs where each asset came from (human-made, AI-generated, purchased) and exports evidence for Steam disclosure and award eligibility.
customer: Indie and mid-size studios (5-100 staff) shipping on Steam, and awards and festival organizers who must adjudicate AI use.
problem: Clair Obscur lost two Indie Game Awards over AI placeholder textures removed before shipping. Eurogamer scored ARC Raiders 2/5 partly over AI voices. Valve requires AI disclosure on Steam. Accusations arrive after launch and the accused have no evidence trail either way.
solution: A local-first logger records per-asset origin (DCC commit hooks, generative-tool API logs, asset-store IDs) into a signed hash chain. It exports an AI Disclosure Report for Steam, award submissions and press, and offers a verifier portal for juries and a public provenance page.
why_now: Award controversies and press scoring now turn on AI use. Steam's disclosure requirement is in force. EA's owners plan AI throughout operations, which will multiply cases.
revenue_model: $15-49 per seat per month, $2-5k per event for awards verification, and $3-10k for forensic audits of accused studios.
non_obvious_insight: The dispute is not AI versus human, it is evidence asymmetry: accusers need no proof and the accused have none. A provenance log protects studios that use AI legitimately (placeholders, disclosed tools) as much as those that do not.
first_30_days: Ship a minimal Blender, Photoshop and Unity logger. Offer it free to awards-eligible entries. Talk to organizers of two indie awards about a verifier pilot, and onboard 20 studios.

title: Retiree Remote-Assist Bench for Robot Fleets
one_liner: A certified, US-based, part-time pool of retirees (ex-truckers, dispatchers, yard hands) who resolve robot and AV exceptions, billed by the assisted hour to fleet operators.
customer: Operators of driverless trucks, yard-automation systems, delivery robots and warehouse fleets (Bot Auto, Gatik, YardFlow-style deployments, sidewalk-robot firms), paying $45-65 per assisted hour.
problem: Every fleet needs remote humans for edge cases. Waymo alone runs about 70 agents on shift, partly in the Philippines, and offshore assist is now a political and first-responder question (NHTSA letter, Jul 2026). Meanwhile 65+ workers want flexible seated income and have the domain judgment, for example reading a truck yard or a weigh station.
solution: Recruit and train retirees on a common exception-handling curriculum. Certify them per vehicle or robot type. Supply them as a managed bench with scheduling, QA and a US-based, background-checked compliance story. Retirees earn $28-40 an hour for 10-20 hours a week, which keeps them under Social Security earnings limits.
why_now: Driverless freight went early-commercial in 2026 (Aurora about 200 trucks, Gatik 85k orders). Fleets are scaling remote-assist headcount, and regulators are scrutinizing where it sits.
revenue_model: Managed-service margin: bill $45-65 per hour, pay $28-40, keep about 35% gross margin. Add training and certification fees per operator.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for autonomy is not more compute. It is cheap, trustworthy human judgment on demand. The demographic everyone treats as a care burden is the best-matched supply of that judgment.
first_30_days: Pitch two mid-size operators for a paid pilot in one metro (freight yards, sidewalk robots). Recruit 25 retired CDL drivers and dispatchers via trucker associations and AARP groups. Run a two-week training and bill the pilot at cost-plus.

title: Cinemas and Arcades as Paid Heat Refuges
one_liner: A standby network of independent cinemas, bowling alleys, arcades and LAN centers that counties activate on heat and smoke days and pay per verified visit.
customer: County and city heat or emergency-management offices, starting with one that has a heat-action plan and a live indoor-temperature mandate (LA County, Maryland counties). Landlords of buildings under indoor temperature caps are the second buyer.
problem: Cooling centers are libraries and rec centers with short hours. Seniors, night-shift workers and teens do not go. Cooling is now a legal duty for landlords: Maryland 80F cap since June 2026, LA County 82F from Jan 2027, NYC 78F from 2030 (secondary sources). When a chiller fails, the fallback is hotel rooms at $150+ a night. Meanwhile independent cinemas, bowling alleys and family entertainment centers sit half-empty on weekday afternoons, with HVAC sized for 300 people.
solution: Pre-contract 20-60 venues per county under a standby agreement. A heat trigger (heat index or WBGT threshold) or smoke trigger (AQI above 150) activates them. On activation, venues open a free-entry lane with water, a screening and a quiet room. Outreach goes out by 211, SMS and health-plan lists, and QR or phone check-in creates per-visit proof. The county pays a standby fee plus a per-verified-visit-hour fee. Landlords can buy prepaid outage passes for tenants when their cooling fails.
why_now: Summer 2026 was reported as the hottest US July on record, and the European heatwave death toll shifted political attention. Cooling mandates are arriving on a 2027-2032 phase-in, so demand is scheduled, not random. FEMA's BRIC money was cancelled, court-restored and then closed to applications on Jul 23 2026, so cities need cheap opex solutions rather than built capacity. Venues want non-ticket revenue.
revenue_model: $150-400 standby fee per venue per heat season, plus $8-15 per verified visit-hour paid by the county. The platform keeps about 25%. Landlord outage passes at $10-15 per tenant-day. Venues keep concession sales.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in a heat emergency is not cold air. It is willingness to go somewhere and stay for six hours. Entertainment venues are dwell-time machines that already hold 300 people at 70F with a reason to stay. Paying only for activated days flips cooling centers from capex to opex with zero idle capacity, and smoke days come free because cinemas can run high-grade filtration.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a heat-action plan and a 2027 budget cycle. Sign LOIs from 5-8 owner-operated cinemas, bowling alleys and arcade bars (phone calls, not enterprise sales). Run an unpaid test activation on the next warm spell or smoke day. Write a one-page cost comparison against hotel vouchers and take it to the county emergency office, one Medicaid managed-care plan and 10 property managers.

title: Translator-Owned Language Trusts for Public Services
one_liner: Translator co-ops that build and license verified medical, legal, and benefits corpora for refugee and diaspora languages, and sell certified human review to agencies that now rely on machine translation.
customer: State Medicaid and benefits agencies, hospital systems, courts, and school districts serving speakers of Karen, Somali, Kirundi, Tigrinya, Haitian Creole, Hmong, Dari, and similar languages. Agencies pay per-word review and $50-150k annual contracts. AI labs and voice-AI vendors license evaluation and fine-tuning data.
problem: General translation is commoditized, so translators are displaced. But in low-resource languages, machine translation of consent forms, discharge instructions, and benefits notices is wrong in dangerous ways, and agencies use it because human capacity has evaporated. Translators' glossaries and corrections are given away or locked in agency-owned translation memories, and gig data platforms pay a pittance.
solution: A member-owned trust per language cluster. Translators contribute and verify domain glossaries and parallel corpora under community governance with consent, revenue share, and veto rights. The trust sells (a) certified human review of machine-translated public-service documents with a warranty, (b) benchmarks and licensed data to vendors, with usage royalties passed to members, and (c) an MT-plus-human-guardrails workflow for agencies.
why_now: The HHS Section 1557 rule (2024) requires qualified human review when machine translation is used on critical health documents, and it remains in effect in 2026, which creates non-discretionary demand. The Mozilla Data Collective opened paid commercial licensing of community datasets and the Gates Foundation has committed to language AI. Freelance translation rates have collapsed.
revenue_model: Per-word certified-review fees, annual agency retainers, data and benchmark licenses, and patronage dividends to member translators.
non_obvious_insight: A translator's most valuable asset is not their time but their error corrections in narrow domains, which is precisely what every model is worst at. The co-op structure solves both community trust and individual freelancers' lack of bargaining power, and legal language-access duties turn the buyer's budget from discretionary to mandatory.
first_30_days: Pick one language and one metro with a large diaspora, such as Karen speakers in St. Paul. Recruit 10-15 translators as founding members. Offer a hospital system or county health department a paid pilot to review its top 50 patient documents against Section 1557 requirements. Build the glossary in shared tooling and sign a governance charter.

title: Error-Rate Cliff Insurance for SNAP Agencies
one_liner: A managed QC service that re-reads a sample of newly approved and recertified SNAP cases against federal review rules and builds federal-dispute packets, sold to county and state agencies facing cost-share penalties.
customer: County social-services directors in county-administered states (NC, CO, MN, NY, OH, VA and others), state QC units, and state agencies with error rates at or above 6%. In FY2025, 20 states were at 10% or higher.
problem: Illinois's FY2025 SNAP error rate was 14.7%. Its DHS estimates roughly $700M of penalty exposure, is hiring 450 staff for $55M, and faces admin costs rising from $60M to $100M as the state share of SNAP admin costs goes from 50% to 75% in October 2026. In North Carolina, Wilson County's DSS (about $13M budget) faces up to $4.2M in penalties with no state relief, and the state's eligibility system (NC FAST) has no document portal or AI. Counties report ~10% vacancy and staff with about a year of experience. Illinois DHS says most errors are 'minor errors', and the federal definition of an error is any variance of $57 or more.
solution: Each week, supervisors upload a 5-10% sample of case files per caseworker. AI extracts income, household composition, deductions and verification documents, recomputes the benefit under federal and state policy, and flags variances of $57 or more with the policy citation. Supervisors get a fix-before-QC list. For cases in the federal QC sample, the tool builds the dispute or arbitration packet comparing the state review with the federal findings. Certified ex-state QC reviewers sign off on anything high-stakes. Deploy inside the county's own cloud tenant so no PII leaves.
why_now: H.R. 1 shifts benefit-cost sharing to states by error-rate tier, with the top tier at 15% of benefit costs for rates of 10% or more. Penalties begin in FY2028-29, starting October 2027 per Capitol News Illinois. The admin-cost shift hits October 2026. Agencies are also absorbing Medicaid work-requirement workloads, so they cannot hire their way to accuracy.
revenue_model: Per-case-reviewed fee ($15-40 range to test) or annual county subscription of $40-150k. For comparison, one county eligibility worker costs $40-95k a year. Optional shared-savings pricing tied to avoided penalty tier.
non_obvious_insight: The penalty is a cliff function by error-rate band, so fixing a handful of cases near a threshold can be worth millions, which makes a cheap second-look service priced like insurance. In county-administered states, each of ~100 counties (NC) is a separate small buyer that carries its own penalty exposure. The cost of the problem is in the evidence: Illinois's 14.7% rate, ~$700M exposure, 450 hires and $55M budget (https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/illinois-food-assistance-error-rate-continues-to-grow-as-federal-penalties-loom/). NC's 10% vacancy, Wilson County's $4.2M penalty exposure on a $13M budget, and staff with 11-13 months' experience (https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2026/04/30/medicaid-work-county-challenges/). Job-posting signal: governmentjobs.com showed about 2,000 'eligibility worker' results on 2026-09-28 at roughly $40-95k salaries (https://www.governmentjobs.com/jobs?keyword=eligibility%20worker). Indiana is hiring 400 people to check eligibility (https://indianacapitalchronicle.com/2026/04/29/fssa-hiring-400-medicaid-eligibility-checkers-ahead-of-work-requirements/) and Pennsylvania has about 400 open county positions (https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-cuts-work-requirements-state-staff-shortages/). Caveat: the tier percentages and FY start dates come from the article and my recollection of the law and should be re-verified.
first_30_days: Target North Carolina, where about 100 counties buy independently in small increments. Recruit 2 retired state QC reviewers as advisers. Offer 3 county DSS directors a free retrospective audit of 100 closed cases, showing errors the county's own review missed. Convert to a paid pilot under the county's small-purchase threshold. Confirm security requirements (in-tenant deployment, redaction) before touching real case files.

title: Employer-Backed Block Leases for Hourly Workers
one_liner: A broker that packages 20-100 unit block leases in concession-heavy buildings, backed by an employer's credit guarantee and payroll deduction, to cut rent for hourly workers without raising wages.
customer: Hospital systems, school districts, hotels, casinos and retailers with recruiting and turnover pain, paired with owners of lease-up and high-concession properties who pay the placement fee.
problem: A typical retail worker earns $34,436 against $71,172 needed for a typical $1,779 apartment. Employers lose workers to housing costs, while owners in lease-up hand out 15-37% concessions to anonymous renters and carry 34 days of vacancy.
solution: Negotiate discounted block rents in exchange for guaranteed occupancy. The employer provides a credit guarantee rather than a subsidy, plus optional payroll deduction, and we run eligibility, lease templates, guarantee underwriting and monitoring. The tenant's discount is funded by the owner's savings on concessions, marketing, vacancy and turnover.
why_now: The rental glut and record concessions give owners a reason to trade price for certainty. Employer labor tightness is high, and traditional locators ignore blocks because commissions are small.
revenue_model: Owner-paid placement fee of 3-4% of first-year rent, employer platform fee of $8-15 per enrolled unit per month, and an optional guarantee premium.
non_obvious_insight: The landlord is buying occupancy certainty, not tenants, and avoided concession, vacancy and turnover can approach 10-15% of annual rent, more than a free month per tenant. Employers can create affordability by lending credit instead of paying wages, which also helps them avoid taxable-benefit complications.
first_30_days: Pick Austin or Atlanta. Get three owners with 300+ unit lease-ups to sign a 10%-off block-lease term sheet. Pitch five HR or recruiting heads at hospital and community-college systems. Run one 25-unit pilot and collect the placement fee.

title: Bind-Ready Binder for Florida Condo Boards
one_liner: One package that coordinates inspections, reserve study and appraisal into a carrier-ready submission, then places the master policy.
customer: Florida condo associations (50-300 units, older buildings), their managers and agents.
problem: SB 4D inspections and reserve-study rules mean carriers want documents before they bind a master policy. Special assessments run $50K-$200K+ per unit, and insurance can be 40-60% of the HOA budget (secondary sources, verify). Boards juggle engineers, reserve-study firms, appraisers and agents separately.
solution: An underwriting package that coordinates the milestone inspection, structural reserve study, insurance appraisal and roof and electrical reports. It produces a carrier-ready binder, places it across 10-plus carriers and E&S markets, and re-certifies annually. The binder is the product, and brokerage is the money.
why_now: Florida's market has flipped and carriers are re-entering. Soft reinsurance rewards well-documented risks with better pricing.
revenue_model: $4-9K package fee per association plus placement commission and referral fees from engineers.
non_obvious_insight: In a softening market, underwriting outcomes are decided by document completeness. The board's problem is coordination, not price.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed agency, sign 5 association managers, and build the binder template from 2 real inspections.

title: Night-Shift Bench Techs for Time-Critical Experiments
one_liner: An agency of vetted, laid-off bench technicians who show up at 2 a.m. or on Christmas morning to harvest time points, feed cells and load overnight runs from the lab's own protocol cards, with photo proof and a break-glass line to the postdoc.
customer: Small private biotechs and startups in shared lab space (LabCentral-type incubators and coworking labs), plus soft-money academic labs with reagent or staffing budgets and industry-funded academic labs. Billed at $85-120/hour with a 2-hour minimum. The incubator or landlord earns a referral fee.
problem: Biology runs on its own clock. 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. time-course harvests, weekend and holiday cell feeding, 48-hour induction windows and overnight instrument runs are the hidden cost of every wet-lab career. Postdocs cover them with sleep debt, guilt-based favors from grad students, or driving in on Christmas. The person who could do it is often laid off, but a lab will not hand $40k of iPSC-derived cells to a stranger, and access badges and insurance make casual help impossible.
solution: A W-2 (employer-of-record) pool of experienced techs, aseptic-technique certified and proven on a practice run, working from the customer's 'protocol cards'. Each shift is a fixed product: Time-Point Harvest, Weekend Split and Feed, Holiday Cover, Overnight Run Loader. Each has a checklist, timestamped photos at every step, a pre-shift 30-minute video walkthrough, and a break-glass contact. Sitters first do a 'dry run' on the customer's cheap spare line. Incubator and coworking-lab operators put the agency on an approved-vendor list, which solves badge and insurance access once for hundreds of labs.
why_now: A large pool of experienced bench techs and postdocs has been released by biotech layoffs since 2023 and funding disruption in 2025-26. Lean startups have fewer people per experiment, so time-critical work lands on founders. Bigger time-course, organoid and perturbation experiments driven by AI-bio data demand make odd-hour work more frequent. Shared-lab operators want more amenities to fill vacant benches.
revenue_model: A markup on billed hours (techs are paid about $40-55/hour, the agency bills $85-120). Monthly retainer for guaranteed availability (for example 'holiday cover pass'). Referral revenue share from shared-lab operators.
non_obvious_insight: The hard constraint is trust, not skill. Nobody outsources their cells because failure is invisible until weeks later. So the product is really an evidence-and-liability wrapper: photo proof, protocol cards, dry runs, and operator pre-approval. Also, the early customers are not academia (IACUC, badges and university procurement kill it) but private benches in rented lab space, where one operator agreement unlocks dozens of labs.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 recently laid-off techs through personal networks and biotech alumni groups. Get a business license, a staffing or PEO partner for payroll, and general liability insurance. Call the community managers at 2-3 shared-lab spaces in one city and offer the first holiday-cover week free. Sell the first paid 3 a.m. harvest to a founder who is already doing it themselves. Turn every job into a reusable protocol card. Aim for about 10 recurring customers by month 6.

title: Tariff Surcharge Credit-Memo Recovery for Mid-Size Manufacturers
one_liner: Mine a plant's accounts-payable history for 2025-26 tariff surcharges, then win credit memos from the distributors who are now receiving IEEPA refunds.
customer: US manufacturers with $5M-$200M revenue and 30-300 active vendors who paid line-item 'tariff surcharges' or tariff-justified price increases from March 2025 through the February 2026 Supreme Court ruling. The buyer is the CFO, controller or purchasing director.
problem: Refunds go to the importer of record, and importers of record are usually distributors: fastener houses, bearing and fitting suppliers, steel service centers, electronics distributors, tooling vendors. The plant paid the surcharge but has no claim with CBP. Downstream buyers have to rely on contract and unjust-enrichment theories against the vendor. Large retailers have law firms doing this, but a $4k-$60k claim per vendor is below any law firm's floor. Plant managers also will not sue the only source of a hydraulic fitting, so the claims are simply going unasked.
solution: 'SurchargeScan': connect to QuickBooks, NetSuite, Epicor or Infor (or upload AP PDFs). AI extracts surcharge lines and tariff-justified price-increase letters, ranks vendors by likelihood of being the importer of record (using public bill-of-lading data and vendor type), and generates reservation-of-rights letters. It then runs a relationship-preserving negotiation for credit memos against future orders instead of cash demands, and tracks each vendor's refund status through CBP's CAPE process. A partner law firm signs off on letters and escalates only large or hostile cases.
why_now: The Supreme Court held the IEEPA tariffs unlawful in February 2026. CBP launched its CAPE refund module on April 20, 2026, with well over $100B accepted for processing. The government is appealing the Court of International Trade's refund order, so vendors are receiving cash now while uncertainty still gives buyers leverage. Every month vendors book the windfall as profit, the claim gets harder to recover.
revenue_model: 20%-25% contingency on recovered credits and cash, plus a $499 scan fee credited against the fee. Average expected recovery of $25k-$150k per plant, with margins on a heavily automated flow. Later, an ongoing 'duty-pass-through audit' for any future tariff regime.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody in the surcharge fight wants to be in court with their own supplier. Plant managers will happily take a credit memo on the next PO but will never file a lawsuit, so the winning product is a diplomatic credit negotiation run by software, not a demand-letter factory.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 Ohio plant controllers as design partners with a free scan in return for 20% on recoveries. Build the scanner with an LLM over exported AP data plus a public bill-of-lading lookup. Send 20 reservation-of-rights letters and get the first credit memos booked. Sign a referral and review agreement with one trade-law boutique. Publish the recovery rate data from the first 10 vendors to sell the next 50 plants.

title: Factory-Slot Exchange for Transformers and Switchgear
one_liner: A verified marketplace and escrow for reassigning manufacturer production slots, the truly scarce asset, from stranded projects to shovel-ready buyers.
customer: Municipal utilities and rural electric co-ops that hyperscaler orders are crowding out, independent power producers, EPC procurement leads, and developers whose projects are stalled by moratoria or interconnection withdrawals and who hold deposit-backed slots they cannot use.
problem: Substation transformer lead times have stretched from about 140 weeks in 2023 to more than 160 weeks in 2026, and medium-voltage gear is at two to three years. Industry estimates say 30-50% of planned 2026 US data center capacity could slip on equipment alone. Slots are reserved years ahead with deposits, and when a project dies (a moratorium, a lost interconnection position) the slot is orphaned. Slot trading happens by handshake in whisper networks, with no verification and no title.
solution: A slot registry plus escrowed transfer. (1) Verify each slot with the manufacturer: spec, kVA and voltage class, delivery window, deposit status. (2) Get manufacturer consent, which is easier if you give them cleaner backlog data. (3) Match buyers using a small technical team of retired utility engineers who know which specs can be re-specified. (4) Hold funds in escrow and transfer title. Publish an index of slot pricing by spec, which is the first public price signal for the shortage.
why_now: Lead times are at record highs in 2026, and new state permit pauses (New York, Texas) are orphaning slots that speculative developers reserved. Small utilities lost their traditional access to equipment as hyperscalers bought capacity, which creates political goodwill for a neutral exchange.
revenue_model: A 2-4% fee on the purchase order value from the buyer and about 1% from the seller. Paid verification dossiers for sellers, and a subscription for the slot price index and alerts.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is the production slot with a spec, not the physical box. Because many slots can be re-specified within tolerance, a technical matchmaker unlocks supply that looks fungible only to insiders. The people hurt most, small utilities, are also the best-motivated and least-served buyers, so serving them is both profitable and defensible.
first_30_days: Recruit two retired utility procurement engineers as advisors. Cold-outreach 50 EPC procurement leads and 20 co-ops (start at NRECA-type meetings and LinkedIn). Collect five slot listings from stalled projects. Broker one transfer manually with a lawyer-drafted escrow agreement and no software. Charge the fee on that deal and use it as proof for the manufacturers.

title: Corridor-Pivot Recruiting for Displaced Gulf Migrants
one_liner: When Gulf jobs disappear, retrain returnees and place them in Japan, Taiwan and Germany with the employer paying the fee.
customer: Employers in care, construction and manufacturing in East Asia and Europe that pay placement fees; the workers pay nothing.
problem: About $50bn of Gulf remittances is at risk. Returnees in Kerala, Nepal, Bangladesh and the Philippines carry recruitment debts and Gulf-specific credentials, and predatory agents will push them into worse corridors.
solution: A skills-credential wallet, language bootcamp and employer-paid placement pipeline, operated through a licensed recruitment partner. The wedge is care workers and welders from Kerala and Nepal for one Japanese or German employer.
why_now: The 2026 Iran-war energy shock displaced workers, and ageing economies are widening visa routes for care and trades.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k employer placement fee per worker, plus employer-paid training subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Displaced migrants are a supply shock nobody is organising. Employer-pays recruitment is both ethical and the direction of ILO fair-recruitment rules.
first_30_days: Sign one Kerala training institute and one overseas care-home operator, and run 30 candidates through a pilot.

title: Parking-Slot Gates for Overrun Villages
one_liner: Sell tiny hotspot villages and trailheads a plate-recognition parking and coach-slot reservation system whose price rises until arrivals fit a hard cap.
customer: Municipalities, mountain and coastal park authorities and private lot operators in places like Alpine lake villages, Dolomites passes, Cinque Terre-type towns and Croatian or Greek islands. Budgets are under EUR 50K, and they already own parking revenue.
problem: Venice's day-tripper fee reportedly did not cut numbers, because a small flat fee is dwarfed by trip cost. Open villages cannot install turnstiles, but almost every day visitor arrives by car, coach or shuttle. Those arrival modes are countable and enforceable, and nobody prices them dynamically.
solution: A cheap camera and plate-recognition kit plus a web app. Visitors reserve parking and coach slots at prices that rise with demand until the cap holds. Residents and overnight guests are exempt through a plate allow-list synced from hotels' check-in data. The cap becomes a subsidy for staying overnight.
why_now: Edge computer vision and plate recognition are now cheap. Record arrivals (1.52B international in 2025) and visible failures of flat fees have made mayors ready to try hard caps. Mount Fuji's 4,000/day cap plus fee shows caps are politically acceptable, and a few Alpine lakes already require reserved road access in peak season.
revenue_model: SaaS of EUR 300-900 per month per site, plus 3-5% of slot fees collected, plus a hardware lease.
non_obvious_insight: Price the arrival mode rather than the person. Cars and coaches are the physical valve for day-trip load, and exempting overnight guests turns a congestion rule into a booking incentive that local hotels will help sell.
first_30_days: Pick 3 villages that already have paid lots. Run a manual pilot with a reservation page and a phone-camera plate check by a local attendant, with no hardware. Sign private lot operators first, since they can decide fastest. Ask mayors for a summer 2027 pilot and a letter of support.

title: Audit-Proof Records for CDL Training Schools
one_liner: A compliance layer that captures entry-level driver training records as training happens, so legitimate CDL school owners survive FMCSA registry purges and audits.
customer: Owners of independent CDL and truck driving schools (roughly 10-500 students a year), whose business depends on staying on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry.
problem: FMCSA has removed thousands of training providers from the registry, put thousands more on notice, and is running in-person audits of roughly 1,500 providers, with Justice Department and DHS attention to fraud in the CDL pipeline. Legitimate small schools with sloppy paperwork (instructor qualifications, curriculum hours, facility and vehicle documentation, timely completion uploads) can lose registration overnight. Students can't test, and the business dies.
solution: A mobile-first record system used on the range and in the classroom. QR or biometric check-in per session, driving-hour and behind-the-wheel logs, instructor qualification and expiry tracking, curriculum completion mapped to the ELDT requirements, and automatic, timely uploads to the registry. It produces an audit binder on demand, runs a mock audit, and offers an audit-day support line.
why_now: The FMCSA crackdown on training providers escalated through 2025-26, and 2026 in-person audits give failing providers about 30 days to fix problems before removal. Owners are frightened, and law firms and generic compliance tools aren't built for a 3-truck school in a strip mall. Carriers increasingly ask where new hires trained.
revenue_model: $299-799 per school per month depending on size. $1,500-3,000 for a one-time audit-readiness package or mock audit. A carrier-paid fee to verify graduates from a 'clean records' school network.
non_obvious_insight: An audit is a documentation exercise, and most schools that fail are honest but disorganized. The registry is a public, scrapeable list, so you can sell to every provider directly by name. Over time the audit-clean data lets you build a trusted graduate-verification network that carriers pay to hire from, which is a bigger business than compliance software alone.
first_30_days: Scrape the public Training Provider Registry list for two or three states. Cold-call and email owners with a free 20-point audit-readiness checklist. Sell a $1,500 audit-readiness package to the first 10 schools. Use their pain points to specify the mobile check-in and logging MVP.
